notes:
I've put together notes on most verses. Searching ran out before I could find sources on verses 30, 36, 37, 39–40, 44 and 47, so those are left out. I didn't reach any Lutheran, Pentecostal, Orthodox, bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org sources, apart from one NET note on v. 38. Guzik's (Enduring Word) chapter page cut off before verse 25, so only his short section summaries are used for the later verses.

**Overview (vv. 25–49)**
- Guzik's summary page says loving enemies is something you do, not a feeling. It also says we must judge ourselves before we correct others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/

**v. 25**
- Guzik: This was an expression of regret and compassion, not a threat. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/
- Ellicott: being "full" means the satiety of over-indulgence. He hears an echo of this verse in James 4:9. https://biblehub.com/luke/6-25.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: the verse is about men who used their wealth for self-indulgence, for the mere gratification of the senses. https://biblehub.com/luke/6-25.htm
- Calvin: the woe falls on people who trust in the good things of this life and turn down heavenly ones. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/6-25.html
- Wesley (Methodist) reads "laugh" as describing people of a light trifling spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/6-25.html
- Desiring God (Piper, Baptist): this must be a different kind of laughing from the joy Jesus commanded in v. 23. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/jesuss-warnings-to-the-comfortable

**v. 26**
- Calvin: this woe is meant to correct ambition. Jesus warns that the approval of other people would ruin his disciples. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/6-26.html
- Barnes: the world opposes Christ's teaching, so if it praises you, that suggests you aren't teaching it truly. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/6-26.html
- Ellicott thinks there may be a particular reference to the time of Hezekiah and the later kings of Judah. https://biblehub.com/luke/6-26.htm
- Poole adds a balance: a good reputation is still worth working for. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/6-26.htm
- Meyer disagrees with the usual reading. He thinks this woe refers to unbelievers, not to disciples. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/6-26.htm

**vv. 27–28**
- Guzik: Jesus defines love for enemies as doing good, blessing and praying. It is a love that acts quite apart from how we might feel about them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/
- Calvin: this one command sums up the whole of the earlier teaching. Someone who loves their enemies will stop seeking revenge. https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol31/htm/ix.li.htm
- Barclay: this love comes from the will as well as the heart. By Christ's grace we can choose to do it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/6-35.html
- Utley (bible.org) notes that this phrase marks a change of audience: these sayings are for disciples, unlike the woes in vv. 24–26. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21303

**v. 29: where traditions differ (non-retaliation versus self-defence)**
- Gill (Baptist) reads it as a proverb. Christ is teaching patience under insult and forbidding private revenge. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/6-29.html
- Wesley (Methodist): it is better to put up with the insult again than to satisfy resentment by setting things right yourself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/6-29.html
- Calvin (Reformed): the words do not stop someone from protecting themselves or their property, as long as they don't take revenge. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/comment3/comm_vol31/htm/ix.xlix.htm
- Desiring God: much of this teaching is hyperbole. Jesus is speaking to individuals, not governments, so self-defence and just war are not ruled out. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/did-jesus-teach-pacifism
- The Expositor's Bible goes furthest. It treats these commands as meant for the disciples' special situation at the time, not as a literal rule today. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/luke-6.html
- Catholic (catholic.com): this site rejects the pacifist reading and offers several possible meanings. One is Aquinas's view that Jesus is teaching patience under insult. https://www.catholic.com/audio/scw/year-a-seventh-sunday-of-ordinary-time

**v. 31**
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) points out that many teachers state the rule negatively, as "don't do what you don't want done to you." Jesus puts it positively. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/6-29.html
- The Expositor's Bible calls the Golden Rule a practical exposition of the Second Commandment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/luke-6.html

**vv. 32–34**
- Benson (Methodist) quotes Theophylact: loving only those who love you makes you like sinners, while loving those who wrong you makes you like God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/6-35.html
- Calvin: Christ asks far more of his people than the ordinary give-and-take of wicked people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/6-35.html

**v. 35**
- Guzik: by doing this we imitate God, who loves his own enemies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/
- Calvin (Reformed) clarifies that nobody *becomes* a child of God by loving enemies. Scripture often describes God's free gifts as rewards to encourage us. https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol31/htm/ix.li.htm
- Clarke (Methodist): this command could never be kept without help from God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/6-35.html
- Translation note from Ellicott: "hoping for nothing again" may be better translated in nothing losing hope. https://biblehub.com/luke/6-35.htm

**v. 38: generosity and the "prosperity" debate**
- Ellicott: the picture is of grain pressed and shaken until the measure can hold no more. The "lap" was the fold of the robe used as a pocket. https://biblehub.com/luke/6-38.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: generosity must be the mark of Jesus' followers. https://biblehub.com/luke/6-38.htm
- Gill (Baptist): the return may come either in temporals or spirituals, or both. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/6-38.htm
- Matthew Henry: God moves other people to give generously to us in turn. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/6-38.html
- Desiring God: the one measuring it back is God himself, not other people. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/just-try-to-outgive-your-god
- On prosperity teaching, a biblehub article says the verse is not strictly a guarantee of material prosperity in return for every gift. https://www.biblehub.com/q/meaning_of_luke_6_38_on_generosity.htm
- NET note (scholarship): the picture comes from measuring grain in the marketplace. The Greek literally says "they will give." https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Luk&chapter=6&tab=commentaries&theme=wiki&verse=38
- Chrysostom and Augustine (early church), as reported in another biblehub article, read the verse as both a warning and a promise. https://biblehub.com/q/What_history_shapes_Luke_6_38_s_meaning.htm

**vv. 41–42**
- Guzik: the speck and plank are deliberately funny exaggerations. Helping a brother with his speck is good, but only after you deal with your own plank. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/
- Utley: classical Greek used the word for "speck" for the bits that make up a bird's nest. https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-6
- Pulpit Commentary applies this to the religious teachers of Jesus' day, whom it calls hypocrites. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/6-41.htm

**vv. 43–45**
- MacLaren: the tree saying states the general rule behind v. 42. Good deeds can only come from a good heart. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/6-41.htm
- Matthew Henry: what we usually say tends to match what fills our heart. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/6-41.htm

**vv. 46–49**
- Guzik: the sermon ends by calling hearers not just to say Jesus' name but to obey him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/
- MacLaren is struck by Christ's bold claim that his words are a rock foundation for any life. He takes the flood to mean the final judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/6-41.htm and https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/luke/three-condensed-parables.cfm
- Gill reads the storm as Satan's temptations, the world's persecution and false teaching. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/6-48.htm
- Vincent: the builder dug through the topsoil and then went deep into the rock. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/6-48.htm
- Text note (Ellicott): the better manuscripts say "because it had been well built." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/6-48.htm
